claims.claim: A written WotC house style guide does exist for the 5e era: 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing', Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast, distributed to freelancers/Adventurers League authors and later bundled on the DMs Guild; it governs mechanics of style, not prose voice.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing v1.04a (PDF, 9 pp.)
claims.quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

claims.claim: The house style rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 16th ed. and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th ed., with the guide covering only D&D-specific departures.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition

claims.claim: Rules text is written in the second person, which the guide presents as the standard way to achieve gender neutrality; singular 'they' is banned outside dialogue and 'he/she' alternation is forbidden.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person

claims.claim: 5e inline subheads (heading 4) end in a period rather than the colon used in earlier editions, e.g. 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency...'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.claim: Game quantities always take numerals ('3 hit points', '1 round', '30 feet') while narrative distances and durations follow Chicago and are spelled out ('fifty miles', 'six hours').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: In rules writing, we use numerals more often.

claims.claim: The guide fixes a verb list for mechanics: you 'make' a saving throw that 'succeeds or fails', attacks 'hit or miss', you 'deal' and 'take' damage, 'regain' hit points, and 'must succeed on' (not 'must make') a check.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.

claims.claim: 5e abandoned the 3E/4E use of 'result' for the number rolled and 4E's 'save' for a successful saving throw; 'magic item' never 'magical item'; 'deals 10 fire damage' not 'points of damage'; 'hit point maximum' not 'maximum hit points'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We have abandoned that practice.

claims.feature: capitalisation and italics of game terms
claims.claim: Ability scores, class features, skills, planes, feats and 'Dungeon Master' are capitalised; spells and magic items are italicised and treated as titles, distinct from the effects they create.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: The italicized terms are treated as titles

claims.claim: The only prose-tone guidance is a 'High Fantasy' paragraph: epic scope, teamwork over lone heroes, humour or tragedy permitted only if they would not seem out of place in Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

claims.claim: American spelling, serial comma required, possessive 's' after names ending in s ('Asmodeus's'), 'non-' hyphenated before fantasy races ('non-elf') but 'nonhuman', 'not' contractions encouraged, vertical lists introduced by a full sentence and colon.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We require the serial comma.

claims.claim: Page references are avoided as error-prone; sections and sidebars are cited by quoted title and chapters by number.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We avoid page references as much as possible.

claims.claim: Dungeon magazine (Paizo era) required read-aloud text to be a bare-bones area description that never references the viewer or presumes player action, banning phrases like 'you see' and 'as you enter the room'.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: it does not make any reference to the viewer

claims.feature: read-aloud text: no creatures, few sentences
claims.claim: Read-aloud text should exclude creatures (whose positions depend on circumstances) and only rarely run more than a few sentences; long descriptive passages belong in player handouts.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: should only rarely run more than a few sentences

claims.claim: The Dungeon house template keys each encounter as header/EL, mandatory Read-Aloud Text first, then General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Development and Treasure, with adventures of 5,000–15,000 words and about 10,000 preferred.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter

claims.claim: Dungeon guidelines tell writers an adventure is not a short story, to condense backstory in favour of PC involvement, and never to presume PC actions or railroad.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: an adventure is not a short story

claims.feature: boxed text length and person (official 5e guidance)
claims.claim: D&D Beyond's official column advises boxed text of roughly four sentences under 100 words, phrased as third-person scene statements rather than 'as you enter, you notice', limited to perceivable sensory detail and excluding PC feelings, villain monologues and non-mechanical game terms.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
claims.quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

claims.claim: Boxed text should describe only what characters perceive, treating everything sensed as 'appears to be' rather than asserting hidden facts.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
claims.quote: Everything they sense 'appears to be' what it is

claims.claim: Chris Perkins says published adventure text should entertain the DM who reads it, seeding humour and Easter eggs so the DM is more inclined to run it, and hooks should appeal to 80–90% of players.
claims.source: Todd Kenreck, 'Chris Perkins on Writing Your Own Adventures', D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19
claims.quote: having had a few good laughs

claims.claim: The WotC House Style Guide bundle circulated to freelancers is summarised as: focus on the characters, include a credible threat, focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
claims.source: Mike Shea, 'On Writing Adventures', Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17
claims.quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.

claims.claim: Boxed text is descriptive text in the adventure book meant to be read aloud verbatim or paraphrased, interleaved with rules references, and the DM-facing text explicitly instructs when to read or skip it.
claims.source: Callison-Burch et al., 'Dungeons and Dragons as a Dialogue Challenge for AI', EMNLP 2022, Appendix B
claims.quote: Read the boxed text when you're ready to start.

claims.claim: McKenzie treats read-aloud text as the adventure's 'at rise' stage direction, typographically set apart and read verbatim, and dates its first appearance to The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, 'D&D Adventures as Tragedy', Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
claims.quote: hints of what may be done are given in this text

claims.feature: DM preference for boxed text (designer poll)
claims.claim: A Jeremy Crawford Twitter poll cited by McKenzie found 59.5% of DMs prefer occasional boxed text, 34.4% want lots, and about 6% want none.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
claims.quote: occasional boxed text

claims.feature: read-aloud text function and NPC action
claims.claim: Grouling Cover describes module read-aloud text as passages the DM is instructed to read that usually describe location but sometimes narrate NPC action, and likens it to a videogame cut-scene.
claims.source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (McFarland 2010), pp. 64–66, 80
claims.quote: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read

claims.claim: Grouling Cover argues second-person address pulls players directly into the storyworld, situating and immersing them, drawing on Fludernik's narratology of second-person texts.
claims.source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (2010), pp. 21, 85
claims.quote: pulling them directly into the storyworld

claims.claim: Hines finds Tomb of Annihilation's text repeatedly uses 'tribal', 'exotic' and 'savage', and its Port Nyanzaru read-aloud leans on vague stereotypes (dinosaurs, bright clothing, click languages) rather than specific cultural detail.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: heavy, characteristic accent

claims.claim: Hines notes DM-facing text instructs voicing Chultans with a heavy accent and tongue clicks, and reads background wording like 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' as prose that frames ruins as needing outsider validation.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: correctly ascertain its original purpose

claims.claim: Hewitt shows Curse of Strahd's Death House read-aloud builds gothic atmosphere through decay adjectives (moldy, rusty, gaunt, pale-faced, voluminous) in present-tense third-person description.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 2024-12-15
claims.quote: festooned with moldy skeletons

claims.claim: Jara analyses rulebooks as framing devices whose covers, prologues, epilogues and embedded fiction shape play; storytelling-game books open with atmospheric prologue fiction, whereas the 1974 D&D booklets used such framing far less.
claims.source: David Jara, 'A Closer Look at the (Rule-) Books', International Journal of Role-Playing 4 (2013)
claims.quote: notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs

claims.claim: Jara coins 'genesic framing' for rulebook text that discloses its own framing and incites players to produce further text, which he says accounts for the medium's persistence.
claims.source: David Jara, IJRP 4 (2013)
claims.quote: what I have called genesic framing

claims.claim: Macdonell argues the 1978 Tomb of Horrors' scripted descriptions and its illustration booklet are dissonant, producing interpretive ambiguity, and that later editions removed the visual assets (abstract only; full text paywalled).
claims.source: Cameron Macdonell, 'Tomes and Tombs', Games and Culture, 2025
claims.quote: visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity

claims.claim: Monte Cook characterises AD&D's house voice as heavy passive voice, stream-of-consciousness digressions, an advanced vocabulary and an authoritative, treatise-like tone that legitimised the hobby.
claims.source: Monte Cook, 'How you say it', Substack, 2021-07-27
claims.quote: the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions

claims.claim: The community term 'High Gygaxian' (coined by Maliszewski) names Gygax's archaic, thesaurus-driven diction ('perforce', 'antithesis of weal'), long multi-clause sentences and baroque tone, fullest in the 1979 DMG and Vault of the Drow.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009-02-19
claims.quote: a platinum word when one worth a copper would do

claims.claim: Akrasia argues AD&D's Latinate vocabulary ('milieu', 'dweomer', 'phantasm', 'eldritch') made difficulty part of the appeal, and that later TSR simplification of the language reduced that cachet.
claims.source: Akrasia, Akratic Wizardry, 2013-03-18
claims.quote: you had to be smarter than average to understand it

claims.claim: A close reading of S1 Tomb of Horrors finds elevated verbs ('precipitated' for dropped), room text that mixes mechanics with narrative so it needs re-reading, yet short punchy details.
claims.source: Gus L, Dungeon of Signs, 2017-04-21
claims.quote: Gygax was good at short punchy bits of detail

claims.claim: Stu Horvath (MIT Press, 2023) calls the 1979 DMG strange and deeply idiosyncratic, a singular authorial vision; Wieck (1989) says the 2e DMG became as much advice as manual; Taylor notes the 5e DMG spends 127 pages teaching a novice DM.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Dungeon Master's Guide' (citing Horvath 2023, Wieck 1989, Taylor/Black Gate)
claims.quote: strange and deeply idiosyncratic

claims.claim: Wikipedia's PHB synthesis records Turnbull (1978) calling OD&D 'ambiguous and muddled' against the coherent AD&D PHB, Schick (1991) on 2e spell descriptions bloating past 100 pages, Kelly (2014) on more polished writing, and Abbott (2024) on the 2014 spell chapter as a wall of text.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Player's Handbook'
claims.quote: an unrelenting wall of text

claims.claim: Games scholar Jaroslav Švelch sees the Monster Manual as modelled on medieval bestiaries but with precise figures; Turnbull praised its explanatory text for amplifying the statistics.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Monster Manual' (citing Švelch, Turnbull)
claims.quote: medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures

claims.claim: The 1977 Monster Manual placed stat lines on the same page as descriptions, and Ed Greenwood criticised Fiend Folio entries for offering strange appearances with no depth to their listings.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Monsters in Dungeons & Dragons'
claims.quote: there is no depth to their listings

claims.claim: Wikipedia credits The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan as the first D&D adventure with boxed read-aloud text, but the citation is a 2017 blog post by Merric Blackman, not a scholarly source.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan'
claims.quote: the first D&D adventure to use boxed

claims.claim: Reviewers cited on Wikipedia find Xanathar's marginal quips too modern in register, sounding like a cranky Redditor rather than a fantasy crime lord.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Xanathar's Guide to Everything' (citing Charlie Hall, Polygon)
claims.quote: feels a bit too modern

claims.claim: Kunzelman (Paste) reads Volo's authorship as a deliberate device letting the sourcebook include rumor and error, and Furniss praises its marriage of narrative and mechanical information.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Volo's Guide to Monsters' (citing Kunzelman, Furniss)
claims.quote: having Volo write the guide means that he can be wrong

claims.claim: A GeekDad reviewer cited on Wikipedia says reading Curse of Strahd front to back is like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book, and Black Gate calls it a setting manual and adventure in one.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Curse of Strahd' (citing Bristol, Jones)
claims.quote: like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book front to back

claims.claim: Evan Torner, cited on Wikipedia, describes 3e's design intent as Eurogame-style elegance in which terminology and choices should be immediately intelligible.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editions of Dungeons & Dragons' (citing Torner)
claims.quote: immediately intelligible to all who might play it

claims.claim: Rhodes argues the 2014 PHB left DMs to guess whether words were ordinary or mechanical, and that the 2024 PHB fixes this by capitalising game mechanics and adding an A–Z Rules Glossary.
claims.source: Duncan Rhodes, Hipsters & Dragons, 2025-03-10
claims.quote: just being used in their normal sense

claims.claim: The official 2024 PHB update renames race to species, 'Cast a Spell action' to 'Magic action', Inspiration to 'Heroic Inspiration', 'Use an Object' to 'Utilize action', folds shoving into Unarmed Strike, and adds glossary entries such as Ally, Enemy, Bloodied and Passive Perception.
claims.source: D&D Beyond staff, 'Updates in the Player's Handbook (2024)', 2024-09-03
claims.quote: Magic action

claims.claim: Screen Rant notes the 2024 Rules Glossary de-emphasises art with monochrome scenes to prioritise text and lacks a dedicated Conditions section.
claims.source: Ben Brosofsky, Screen Rant, 2024-09-21
claims.quote: the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions

claims.claim: Arndt reports the 2025 Monster Manual cuts iconic monsters' multi-page lore to at most three paragraphs and a roll table, adds a subtitle epithet to every monster, renames phylactery to 'spirit jar', and reads as a utilitarian encyclopedia.
claims.source: Dan Arndt, The Fandomentals, 2025-01-28
claims.quote: three paragraphs and a table to roll on

claims.claim: Shank's MA thesis characterises campaign-setting handbooks as giving encyclopedic knowledge of D&D geography, history and politics alongside ancillary rules.
claims.source: Nathan Shank, 'The Narrative Structures of Dungeons and Dragons', MA thesis 2011 (academia.edu, abstract/intro only)
claims.quote: encyclopedic knowledge of D&D geography, history, and politics

claims.claim: No stylometric, corpus-linguistic or authorship-attribution study of official D&D prose was found; searches on those terms returned only NLP actual-play datasets and generic stylometry papers, and the term 'Gygaxian' does not surface in Analog Game Studies, Games and Culture or IJRP indexes.
claims.source: Negative result from this sweep (searches 3, 22, 25, 35; Semantic Scholar rate-limited)

0.trueWording: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing
0.note: Page 1 title line reads exactly 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing'; footer on every page reads 'Version 1.04a (c)2013 Wizards of the Coast'; PDF is 9 pages, matching '9 pp.'. CAVEAT: the document itself says nothing about distribution to freelancers/Adventurers League authors or later DMs Guild bundling - that provenance is unverified by the source (only circumstantial: the host is adventurersleague.wordpress.com). Also 'governs mechanics of style, not prose voice' is nearly but not wholly true: a 'High Fantasy' section gives tone guidance (see index 8).

1.trueWording: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition
1.note: Page 1: 'We have two primary resources for the house style of DUNGEONS & DRAGONS products: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition / Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary, 11th edition.' Minor overstatement in the claim: the guide says it focuses on matters 'where we depart from or expand on' those works, so 'only D&D-specific departures' understates the 'expand on' half. New Oxford American Dictionary is named as a third, backup resource.

2.trueWording: In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.
2.note: Quote is a contiguous substring of the page-2 sentence. All three sub-claims confirmed: 'Don't use "they" or "their" as singular pronouns, except in an informal context like dialogue'; 'avoid "he/she" and "s/he" altogether'; 'don't alternate between "he" and "she"'. CAVEAT: the guide hedges with 'often', so 'presents as the standard way' is slightly stronger than the source.

3.trueWording: Contrary to past D&D usage, this subhead should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon.
3.note: Page 2 'Inline Subheads': 'The lowest level of our heading hierarchy is the inline subhead. It functions as our heading 4.' The correct/incorrect example pair is verbatim: 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency in the Perception skill.' vs 'Keen Senses: ...'. CAVEAT: the guide permits any terminal punctuation - 'Use a period, an exclamation point, or a question mark' - so 'end in a period' is narrower than the rule.

4.trueWording: Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.
4.note: Every example in the claim is verbatim in the source: 'Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points'; 'The spell lasts for 1 round'; 'The attack has a range of 30 feet'; and under 'But:' - 'The two cities are fifty miles apart' and 'After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.' The general rule cited is Chicago 9.2 (spell out zero to one hundred). 'always' is a shade stronger than the guide's framing but the substance holds.

5.trueWording: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.
5.note: Page 6 'Verb Usage' list carries all of it verbatim: 'You deal damage.' / 'You take damage.' / 'You regain hit points.' / 'You make an attack (or you attack), and your attack hits or misses (it doesn't succeed or fail).' CAVEAT on 'must succeed on (not must make)': the ban is conditional - 'Don't write, "You must make a DC 15 Strength check..." unless that sentence is immediately followed by a description of what happens on a success or failure.' Separately, for effects imposing a save the guide actually PREFERS 'the target must make a saving throw'.

6.note: The sentence appears twice, verbatim, once for each abandonment: under 'Saving Throws' ('In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.') and under '"Result" and Die Rolls' ('In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die." We have abandoned that practice.'). Also confirmed: '"magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item"'; 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage"'; 'When you write about a creature's hit point maximum, avoid "maximum hit points."'

7.trueWording: The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.
7.note: 'Terms to Capitalize' lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, Traits. 'Terms to Italicize' lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells. The distinctness point is verbatim: 'Don't confuse one of these titles with an effect it creates... the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire, not a wall of fire.' Note artifacts are BOTH capitalized and italicized.

8.trueWording: there are moments of humor with the hobbits, but ring wraiths aren't used for gags
8.note: Quote is verbatim apart from the source's curly apostrophe in 'aren't'. The 'High Fantasy' section confirms epic scope ('the epic scope characteristic of that subgenre') and teamwork ('The lone knight fighting a dragon is less characteristic of D&D than an adventuring team fighting a dragon'). CAVEAT: the LotR/Game of Thrones test is framed as a 'When in doubt' heuristic, not the permission condition - the stated condition is that humor/tragedy be 'true to the facts of the brand and don't overtake the general tone'. 'The only prose-tone guidance' is the reviewer's inference, but it survives a read of all 9 pages: no other voice or register section exists.

9.note: All six sub-claims confirmed verbatim: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; the serial-comma sentence; 'We write "Asmodeus's lair," not "Asmodeus' lair"'; 'non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's)'; 'We encourage the use of contractions formed with "not"'; 'introduce it with a complete sentence ended by a colon' for vertical lists.

10.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible.
10.note: Continues 'They are labor-intensive (they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error.' Cross-reference style confirmed: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number' and 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes.' One refinement: a table title is explicitly NOT enclosed in quotes.

11.trueWording: Read-aloud text provides a bare-bones description of the encounter area; it does not make any reference to the viewer.
11.note: Verbatim on the page (page 12-13 boundary); my PDF text extractor merely dropped the space at the 'it / does' line break. Next sentence is verbatim too: 'Avoid phrases such as "you see," "as you enter the room," or other phrases that assume any action whatsoever on behalf of the players.' Paizo attribution confirmed by the document itself: byline 'By the DUNGEON Staff', address 'DUNGEON Magazine, Paizo Publishing, 2700 Richards Road, Suite 201, Bellevue, WA'. Era is 3.5e (cites Monster Manual II, Fiend Folio, Draconomicon, DUNGEON #114).

12.trueWording: Read-aloud text for an encounter should only rarely run more than a few sentences.
12.note: Both halves verbatim and adjacent: 'You should also avoid including descriptions of any creatures in the room, since their activities and positions in the room often depend on multiple factors (such as if they hear the PCs coming, if it's night or day, and so on).' and 'Long sections of read-aloud text are better served as player handouts.'

13.trueWording: Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development, and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment
13.note: Quote IS verbatim ('This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter, although part of the general description might precede it if important to the encounter.'), and the header/EL and word-count halves are confirmed verbatim: 'Each encounter should be rated with an Encounter Level (EL #) in the main encounter header'; sample header '23. Vampire's Den (EL 13)'; 'Our adventures typically range from 5,000 to 15,000 words in length'; 'we automatically reject any adventure manuscript that contains fewer than 5,000 or more than 15,000 words. The ideal manuscript size is 10,000 words.' DOWNGRADED because the claim's section order is wrong: the source order is Treasure BEFORE Development, and the claim omits Trap(s) and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment from a list it presents as the template. Also 'mandatory Read-Aloud Text' needs care - the heading is labelled (Mandatory) in the template, but the encounters paragraph says 'Each encounter can include any or all of the following sections... Do not include sections that are unnecessary for a given encounter.'

14.trueWording: Regardless of how cool your backstory is, an adventure is not a short story.
14.note: Quote verbatim in the query-writing tips. Continues: 'You need to condense or sacrifice background description in favor of telling us about PC involvement. It's how the adventure PLAYS that determines whether or not a proposal is something we want to pick up.' The adventure should be flexible enough for PCs to make choices and decisions that could affect the outcome of the story. Avoid rigid timelines.' The design guide adds 'The Adventure Background section should be no more than 5% of the total length of the adventure.'
